top.s: Personally I'm always happier somewhere up in the hills with a bit of a chill in the air, I just feel more awake there.
For what it's worth, I absorb stuff way better from diagrams than from walls of text, so wherever a picture would do, lean on that.
Our convention on this team is that every bug fix ships with a regression test first, no exceptions, so whatever we do needs to fit that.
Speeches make me incredibly nervous, so I'd rather keep it short — three minutes, tops — and something I can mostly read without sounding like I'm reading.
Our data team is two people, so anything that needs a dedicated platform engineer is a non-starter.
I've cut out red meat completely for about a year now and don't miss it, chicken and fish are fine.

I've read a bit about async reviews with Loom and about smaller "design pairs." When I plan anything like this I like having two options to choose between rather than one recommendation, it helps me think.
I always write first drafts in present tense; it keeps me close to the character.
Heads up, I'm pretty new to Go (came from years of Java), so if something looks un-idiomatic, call it out and explain why instead of just rewriting it.

I went through it with the team this morning and it's mostly right, but I ended up rewriting the whole rollout section before I could share it — it assumed we'd do a big-bang cutover over a weekend, and we just don't do that here; everything goes out behind a gradual percentage rollout with a kill switch, which is the third time I've had to fix that in something you've drafted.
It was useful but I had to cut it down a lot before sending to the leadership group — they're not going to read eleven bullet points with sub-bullets, and honestly neither am I most days.
You wrote the examples in Java again — I've mentioned our stack is Kotlin and it's a bit annoying translating every snippet in my head, especially the null-handling bits which don't map one to one.
